title: Solubility Equilibrium
standard_text: Saturated solutions are systems in equilibrium: solubility, the solubility product Ksp, molar solubility, predicting precipitates with the trial ion product, and the common ion effect. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Chemistry 12)
meta_desc: Free Chemistry 12 worksheets (BC Curriculum): Ksp, molar solubility and precipitation. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A saturated solution is at equilibrium.
key_sub: Trial ion product > Ksp → a precipitate forms.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a saturated solution of a slightly soluble salt, the dissolving and precipitating rates are equal. For AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]. For a salt AB, Ksp = s²; for AB₂, Ksp = 4s³.

To predict a precipitate, calculate the trial ion product Q: if Q > Ksp, a precipitate forms. Adding a common ion lowers the solubility of a salt (the common ion effect).

Example

The molar solubility of AgCl is 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ mol/L. What is its Ksp?

Ksp = s²

Answer: 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁰

Example

Q = 2 × 10⁻⁸ and Ksp = 1 × 10⁻¹⁰. Does a precipitate form?

Compare Q and Ksp.

Answer: yes

Common mistakes

  • Using s² for every salt.
  • Forgetting to account for dilution when solutions are mixed.
  • Thinking a common ion increases solubility.

faq.q: Why is a small Ksp a sign of low solubility?
faq.a: Very few ions are in solution at equilibrium.

faq.q: How are precipitates used to treat water?
faq.a: Unwanted ions such as phosphate are removed as insoluble salts.
